There have been various proposals to expand the G7. The U.S.-based Atlantic Council has held the [D-10 Strategy Forum](/wiki/D-10_Strategy_Forum "D-10 Strategy Forum") since 2014 with representatives from what it calls "leading democracies" which support a "rules-based democratic order", consisting of all members of the G7 (including the [European Union](/wiki/European_Union "European Union")) plus [Australia](/wiki/Australia "Australia") and [South Korea](/wiki/South_Korea "South Korea"). Several democratic countries – including [India](/wiki/India "India"), [Indonesia](/wiki/Indonesia "Indonesia"), [Poland](/wiki/Poland "Poland"), and [Spain](/wiki/Spain "Spain") – participate as observers.[[32]](#cite_note-auto1-32) Centered around a similar mandate as the G7, the D-10 has been considered by some analysts to be an alternative to the group;[[33]](#cite_note-:0-33) This is also favored by various [think tanks](/wiki/Think_tank "Think tank") and former [British leader Boris Johnson](/wiki/Boris_Johnson "Boris Johnson").[[32]](#cite_note-auto1-32)

In 2019 under [Putin](/wiki/Vladimir_Putin "Vladimir Putin"), [Russia](/wiki/Russia "Russia") had signaled support for the inclusion of [China](/wiki/China "China"), India, and [Turkey](/wiki/Turkey "Turkey") if the G7 had reinstated Russian membership.[[34]](#cite_note-34)

In 2020 under [Trump](/wiki/Donald_Trump "Donald Trump"), the U.S. had signaled support for the inclusion of Australia, [Brazil](/wiki/Brazil "Brazil"), India, and South Korea, plus the reincorporation of Russia.[[35]](#cite_note-35)[[36]](#cite_note-36) The leaders of the other six G7 members unanimously rejected this proposal.[[37]](#cite_note-37)

Also in November 2020, [Jared Cohen](/wiki/Jared_Cohen "Jared Cohen") and [Richard Fontaine](/wiki/Richard_Fontaine "Richard Fontaine"), writing in *[Foreign Affairs](/wiki/Foreign_Affairs "Foreign Affairs")*, suggested that the G7 might be expanded to a "T-12" of "Techno Democracies". The capital and the largest city of the province is [Harbin](/wiki/Harbin "Harbin"). Among Chinese provincial-level [administrative divisions](/wiki/Administrative_divisions_of_China "Administrative divisions of China"), Heilongjiang is the [sixth-largest by total area](/wiki/List_of_Chinese_administrative_divisions_by_area "List of Chinese administrative divisions by area"), the [20th-most populous](/wiki/List_of_Chinese_administrative_divisions_by_population "List of Chinese administrative divisions by population"), and the [second-poorest by GDP per capita](/wiki/List_of_Chinese_provincial-level_divisions_by_GDP_per_capita "List of Chinese provincial-level divisions by GDP per capita") after only [Gansu](/wiki/Gansu "Gansu") province.

The province takes its name from the [Amur](/wiki/Amur "Amur") river which marks [the border](/wiki/China%E2%80%93Russia_border "China–Russia border") between the [People's Republic of China](/wiki/People%27s_Republic_of_China "People's Republic of China") and [Russia](/wiki/Russia "Russia").

Heilongjiang has significant agricultural production,[[6]](#cite_note-Stratfor-7) and raw materials, such as timber, oil, and coal.

The province takes its name from the [Amur](/wiki/Amur "Amur") river, whose name in [Mandarin](/wiki/Mandarin_Chinese "Mandarin Chinese") is *Heilongjiang* ('black [dragon](/wiki/Chinese_dragon "Chinese dragon") river').[[7]](#cite_note-:12-8)
